abstract: Experience-dependent plasticity is fundamental to adaptive behaviour, yet the conditions under which basic sensory timing can be modified in adulthood remain poorly specified. Critical flicker fusion frequency (CFFF), the threshold at which flicker is perceived as continuous, is unusually informative here: what fails to change it is as well documented as what does. We argue that CFFF is best characterised neither as non-plastic nor as held near a physiological ceiling, but as modifiable only by a specific class of experience, not by amount. Repeated testing changes it little, and cognitive training without temporal content and incoherent-motion exposure leave it unchanged regardless of duration. By contrast, perceptual-learning paradigms that repeatedly drive early visual processing of transient signals can raise it. The evidence is graded: strongest for task-irrelevant coherent motion temporally paired with task targets, with one-year retention in a small subsample; weaker for contrast and dot-motion training; and, for flicker training, confined to amblyopic eyes starting below typical values. Three qualifications apply: samples are small; the motion and contrast paradigms were assessed with a small foveal stimulus on a macular pigment densitometer, whose equivalence with standard CFFF measurement is unestablished; and a minority of untrained controls show comparable changes. We examine whether the restriction originates at peripheral, thalamocortical, or cortical levels; available data do not adjudicate between them. Functional arguments for such a restriction are offered as rationales, not evidence. Proposed links to working-memory precision and metacognition are stated as predictions; first tests were largely negative.
